summary: Defines the notation used to state what a management implementation must support and what it actually does support. This helps describe minimum requirements and the level actually achieved. It was replaced by RFC 2580.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1904 defines how SNMPv2 MIB files describe their own requirements. Four kinds of statement are supported: a group of related objects, a group of related notifications, the minimum a conforming implementation of a module must do, and what one particular agent really supports, including where it differs from the written definition.

how do mib modules describe compliance
subtitle: The notation SNMPv2 MIB modules use to say what an implementation must do, and what one agent actually does.

tldr.problem: A MIB module describes what a device may expose, but a reader also needs to know the minimum a conforming implementation must provide and what a particular agent really provides.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four ASN.1 macros: two that name groups of objects and notifications, one that states a module's minimum requirements, and one that records an agent's own capabilities, bound to the value of its sysORID.
tldr.outcome: Together they let a vendor and a customer state, in a machine-readable way, what is required and what is delivered. RFC 1904 has been obsoleted by RFC 2580 and is no longer current.

today: RFC 1904 has been obsoleted by RFC 2580, so it is no longer a current standards document. It was published in January 1996 as a Draft Standard, and it had itself obsoleted RFC 1444.

sections.title: Why Conformance Statements Exist
sections.content:
A management system contains several, potentially many, nodes, each with a processing entity called an agent that has access to management instrumentation; at least one management station; and a management protocol used to convey management information between the agents and the stations. Operations of the protocol are carried out under an administrative framework that defines authentication, authorization, access control and privacy policies.

The management stations run management applications that monitor and control managed elements, which are devices such as hosts, routers and terminal servers. Management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects, residing in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base, the MIB. Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules, written using a subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One called the Structure of Management Information.

It may be useful to define the acceptable lower bounds of implementation, along with the actual level of implementation achieved, and it is the purpose of this document to define the notation used for those two purposes. The RFC notes the terminology it uses: the original Internet-standard Network Management Framework of RFCs 1155, 1157 and 1212 is called the SNMP version 1 framework, and the current one the SNMP version 2 framework.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB file lists the values a device can expose. That is not enough on its own: a reader also needs to know the smallest set a conforming product must offer, and how a particular product differs from the written description. This RFC provides the words for both.

sections.title: The Four Macros
sections.content:
Everything in this RFC is expressed through four ASN.1 macros, defined in a module called SNMPv2-CONF. In each case the expansion of the macro happens during implementation and not at run time, so a device never has to compute anything from these clauses.

OBJECT-GROUP names a collection of related managed objects, and its OBJECTS clause, which must be present, lists them. Every object named must be defined in the same information module as the macro appears, and must have a MAX-ACCESS value of accessible-for-notify, read-only, read-write or read-create. One rule exists to catch a common mistake: every object defined in an information module with a MAX-ACCESS other than not-accessible must be contained in at least one object group, so that a new object cannot be added to a module and forgotten in the groups.

NOTIFICATION-GROUP is the same shape for notifications, with a NOTIFICATIONS clause naming each one, each defined in the same information module.

MODULE-COMPLIANCE conveys a minimum set of requirements for implementing one or more MIB modules. Every standard MIB module must have a corresponding MODULE-COMPLIANCE specification, either in the same information module or in a companion one.

AGENT-CAPABILITIES conveys a set of capabilities present in one agent.

The first three macros share a STATUS clause, which must be present and takes the values current, deprecated or obsolete. Deprecated means the definition is obsolete but an implementor may wish to support the group to foster interoperability with older implementations. They also share a DESCRIPTION clause, which must be present and gives a textual definition, though generic compliance requirements should not be stated there, and a REFERENCE clause, which need not be present and cross-references a statement in another information module, which is useful when converting a MIB module produced by another organisation. The AGENT-CAPABILITIES macro instead has a PRODUCT-RELEASE clause, which must be present and names the product release that has these capabilities, and its STATUS takes only current or obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: Four building blocks do the work. Two bundle related things together, one says what a module demands, and one says what a particular product delivers. Each carries a status, a description and, usually, a pointer to the document it came from.

sections.title: Conformance Groups and Notification Groups
sections.content:
To implement an object, an SNMPv2 entity acting in an agent role must return a reasonably accurate value for management protocol retrieval operations; and if the object is writable, it must be able to influence the underlying managed element in response to a set operation. If an agent cannot implement an object, the management protocol lets it return an exception or error such as noSuchObject. Under no circumstances shall an entity return a value for an object it does not implement: it must always return the appropriate exception or error.

The OBJECTS clause of an OBJECT-GROUP names each object in the group, and the STATUS and DESCRIPTION clauses work as described above. The value of an OBJECT-GROUP invocation is the name of the group, an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name. The RFC's example is the SNMP Group, which lists seven objects and is described as a collection of objects providing basic instrumentation and control of an SNMPv2 entity.

The NOTIFICATION-GROUP macro works the same way with notifications. Its example, the SNMP Basic Notifications Group, names two notifications, coldStart and authenticationFailure, and is described as the two notifications an SNMPv2 entity is required to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: A group is a named bundle of objects or of notifications, and each one says whether it is current, deprecated or obsolete. The rule about objects is strict: an agent must return a real value for what it claims to support, and an explicit error for what it does not, never a made-up value.

sections.title: Module Compliance: The Minimum Bar
sections.content:
The MODULE-COMPLIANCE macro states the minimum requirements for implementing one or more MIB modules. Its MODULE clause, which must be present, is repeated to name each MIB module the requirements apply to, by module name and optionally by OBJECT IDENTIFIER. The module name may be omitted when the invocation sits inside a MIB module, in which case it refers to the enclosing one.

The MANDATORY-GROUPS clause, which need not be present, names the groups within that module which are unconditionally mandatory. If an agent claims compliance with the module, it must implement every object and notification in every listed group. If it returns a noSuchObject exception for any object in a mandatory group for every MIB view, or cannot generate each notification in any group under the appropriate circumstances, then it is not a conformant implementation of that module.

The GROUP clause, which need not be present, names groups that are conditionally mandatory or unconditionally optional. A group named here must be absent from the MANDATORY-GROUPS clause. Conditionally mandatory groups are those that are mandatory only if a particular protocol is implemented, or only if another group is implemented, and the DESCRIPTION of the clause states the conditions. A group named in neither clause is unconditionally optional.

The OBJECT clause, which need not be present, names individual objects whose compliance requirement is refined. The object must already appear in one of the groups named by the mandatory or group clauses. The refinement may give a SYNTAX for reading, a WRITE-SYNTAX for writing, and a MIN-ACCESS giving the minimal level of access. If MIN-ACCESS is absent the minimal level is the maximal level from the object's own definition; if present it must not be greater. The access level of certain kinds of object is fixed by its syntax, including conceptual tables and rows, auxiliary objects and objects with the syntax of Counter32 or Counter64, and a MIN-ACCESS clause should not be present for those. An implementation is compliant when the access it provides is at least the minimal level and no more than the maximal one.

The RFC's example is a hypothetical compliance statement that makes five groups mandatory and one group, xyzV1Group, mandatory only for entities that also implement XYZv1.
sections.plainLanguage: A compliance statement says what a product must do to claim it follows a module. Some groups are simply required; others are required only in certain conditions; others are optional. Individual objects can have their access or their data type tightened or loosened within limits.

sections.title: Agent Capabilities: What Was Actually Built
sections.content:
When a MIB module is written it is divided into units of conformance termed groups, and if an agent claims to implement a group it must implement every object in that group. An entity might implement only a subset of the groups in a module, and the definition of some objects leaves aspects to the discretion of the implementor.

Practical experience has shown a need to describe an agent's capabilities concisely with respect to one or more MIB modules. The AGENT-CAPABILITIES macro lets an agent implementor describe the precise level of support the agent claims for a MIB group, and bind that description to the value of an instance of sysORID. Some objects may have restricted or augmented syntax or access levels.

Given such an invocation, a management station implementor can build management applications that optimise themselves when talking to a particular agent. The station can keep a database of these invocations, retrieve the values of all instances of sysORID from the agent it is talking to, look up the matching entries, and adjust its behaviour accordingly. The RFC notes that the macro describes refinements or variations with respect to the OBJECT-TYPE and NOTIFICATION-TYPE macros in MIB modules, not with respect to MODULE-COMPLIANCE macros.

Each SUPPORTS clause names a MIB module for which the agent claims a complete or partial implementation, and its INCLUDES clause, which must be present for each use of SUPPORTS, names the groups the agent claims to implement. The VARIATION clause, which need not be present, names objects or notifications the agent implements in a variant or refined way. It may narrow the SYNTAX or WRITE-SYNTAX, and its ACCESS clause says that the agent provides less than the maximal level of access. The only value applicable to notifications is not-implemented, which means the agent does not implement the object or notification and, in the ordering of possible values, is equivalent to not-accessible. The value write-only exists only for backward compatibility and must not be used for newly defined object types. A CREATION-REQUIRES clause names the columnar objects of a conceptual row that must be given values before the agent will allow the row's status column to be set to active, and a DEFVAL clause gives a refined default value.

The value of an AGENT-CAPABILITIES invocation is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER naming the value of sysORID for which the statement is valid. The RFC's example is an agent for 4BSD that supports six MIB modules, with variations such as ifAdminStatus restricted to a smaller syntax, ipInAddrErrors marked not-implemented, and tcpConnState available for reading only.
sections.plainLanguage: The compliance statement says what the module demands. The capabilities statement says what this product does, including the places where it is narrower: an object it does not have, one it can only read, or one whose values are restricted. It is tied to a value the agent publishes, so a manager can look it up and adapt.

sections.title: Extending an Information Module
sections.content:
As experience is gained with a published information module it may be desirable to revise it. Section 10 of the Structure of Management Information defines the rules for extending an information module, and the rest of this section says how conformance groups, compliance statements and capabilities statements may be extended. For all three the rule is the same: if any non-editorial change is made to any clause of the statement, the OBJECT IDENTIFIER value associated with it must also be changed, along with its associated descriptor.

The RFC has a short security section, and it consists of one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: When a published MIB module is revised, anything more than a wording change means the identifier of the affected group, compliance statement or capabilities statement has to change too, so that old and new versions can be told apart.

viz.caption: THE FOUR MACROS AND WHAT EACH ONE STATES

items.title: OBJECT-GROUP
items.text: Names a set of related managed objects. Every object a module defines, other than one that is not accessible, must be in at least one group.

items.title: NOTIFICATION-GROUP
items.text: Names a set of related notifications, such as the traps an agent is required to send.

items.title: MODULE-COMPLIANCE
items.text: States the minimum requirements for implementing one or more MIB modules, with mandatory groups, conditional groups and refinements for individual objects.

items.title: AGENT-CAPABILITIES
items.text: States what one particular agent implements, including the objects it narrows, restricts or does not implement at all.

viz.caption: THE COMPLIANCE STATEMENT EXAMPLE FROM THE RFC

data.title: A MODULE-COMPLIANCE statement
data.code:
xyzMIBCompliance MODULE-COMPLIANCE
    STATUS  current
    DESCRIPTION
            "The compliance statement for XYZv2 entities which implement
            the XYZv2 MIB."
    MODULE  -- compliance to the containing MIB module
        MANDATORY-GROUPS { xyzSystemGroup,
                           xyzStatsGroup, xyzTrapGroup,
                           xyzSetGroup,
                           xyzBasicNotificationsGroup }

        GROUP   xyzV1Group
        DESCRIPTION
            "The xyzV1 group is mandatory only for those
             XYZv2 entities which also implement XYZv1."
::= { xyzMIBCompliances 1 }
